title: Errors in a support inbox
excerpt: A failed reply must say whether the customer saw it, and it must keep the draft. Timeouts, bad attachments, and a second agent sending at the same time need different sentences.
alt: Hands sketching a user-flow diagram labeled user goals on a sheet of paper, tracing what the agent does when a send fails.
caption: The recovery is a path, drawn before the outage. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What is the first thing a failed reply should say?
faqs.answer: Whether the customer saw the message. If it did not send, keep the text and the attachments in the composer. If you are not sure, do not mark the conversation answered. A toast that disappears, and a composer that clears, will force the agent to retype.

faqs.question: How should a collision be written?
faqs.answer: Say who else sent a reply, keep the draft, and ask the agent to read before sending. That is not a network failure. A generic conflict dialog that discards the draft will push careful replies into a side document.

faqs.question: What if only the sidebar fails?
faqs.answer: Leave the open thread alone and say the list could not refresh. If the thread itself fails, keep the customer's name and offer a retry. An empty inbox that looks like the work vanished is a worse error than the one you started with.

markdown:
Clear support inbox error states tell the agent what broke, whether the customer saw the reply, and the next step that repairs it. A code and a sad illustration waste the minute the customer is still waiting in.

The W3C's WCAG overview groups its guidelines under perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. A failed send has to be perceivable as text, and understandable as a recovery. A red bubble with no sentence meets neither.

## Did the customer see it

This is the only question that matters first. The agent needs one of three answers, in words on the thread.

- The reply was delivered.
- The reply was not delivered, and it is still in the draft.
- You do not know yet, and the thread says how they will know.

"Something went wrong" with the composer's contents cleared is the worst version, because you have destroyed the recovery. Keep the text. Keep the attachments. Say the send failed. Let them send again without retyping a careful apology.

If the message left your system and the customer's mail server rejected it, say that the customer did not see it, and name the dull reason if you have it. "Their inbox refused the message. Check the address, or try the other email on the account." If it left your system and you have no receipt, say you are not sure, and do not mark the conversation as answered. A green check that is really a guess will drop the thread out of the queue while the customer is still waiting.

Put the sentence on the message, not in a toast that vanishes. Toasts are easy to miss when the agent is already reading the next ticket. The failed reply should stay in the thread, visually distinct from messages the customer received, until it is sent or discarded on purpose.

## The send, the attachment, and the collision

Split the failures. A network timeout, a rejected attachment, and another agent sending at the same time are different recoveries, and they need different sentences.

A timeout: "Not sent. Your text is still here. Try again." Disable the extra clicks while the first try is in flight, so a double send is not the next error. If the first try actually landed and the client never heard, the retry must not create a second email. Idempotent sends are a product requirement, not a backend nicety. The screen should still assume the agent is anxious and will tap twice.

An attachment: "The file was not sent. Replies can include files up to the limit you set, and this one is larger. The text was not sent either," if that is true. Do not send the text and drop the file in silence, or the customer gets an answer that refers to a photo they never received. Say which part failed. Offer to send the text alone only as an explicit choice.

A collision: "Sam sent a reply while you were writing. Read it before you send yours." Keep their draft. Show Sam's message above it. This is not a failure of the network. It is a failure of coordination, and the words should sound like it. A generic "conflict" dialog that discards the draft will train agents to paste important replies into a notes app first, which means your inbox is no longer where the work happens.

## Addresses, macros, and the channel

A wrong address should be caught before the send when you can know, and explained after when you cannot. "This conversation is email, and the address is missing a domain." Inline, on the field, in the same voice as the thread. If the customer wrote from a channel that cannot receive a reply, say that before the agent types for five minutes. "This review was pulled in from a public page. A reply here will not reach them. Use the email on the order."

Macros fail when a token is empty. "This reply still contains the blank where the order number goes. The customer has no order on the account." Do not send a sentence with a hole in it. Highlight the hole. Let the agent fill it or pick a different reply. A macro that sends "{{tracking_number}}" to a real person is an error you should be ashamed to ship, and it is preventable with a check you can explain.

Channel switches fail too. The agent thinks they are replying by email and the product sends a chat message to a widget the customer closed, or the reverse. The button has to name the channel. If the channel becomes impossible mid-compose, keep the draft and change the button's sentence. "Chat is closed. Send as email to jess@… instead." Make that a choice, not a silent reroute.

## The queue can fail without the reply failing

The list and the thread are different objects. If the thread is open and the list cannot refresh, say so on the list and leave the thread alone. The agent can finish the reply in front of them. A full-page error that throws away a composed answer, because a sidebar query timed out, is a design defect.

If the thread itself cannot load, keep the row they clicked and say you could not open it. Offer retry. Do not drop them on an empty inbox that looks like the work vanished. "Could not open Mina's conversation. It is still in your queue." The name matters. A nameless failure feels like data loss.

Assignment can fail. "You could not take this, because Sam took it a moment ago." Show Sam's name and leave the conversation readable. Taking and failing should not look like a send failure. The customer is not involved yet. The words should not imply they were.

Search and filters create false errors. An inbox filtered to "mine" that hides a conversation the agent just assigned away is not a bug, but it looks like one if you do not say "Filtered to you. This conversation is now with Sam." Empty because of a filter gets a sentence. Empty because the queue is clear gets a different sentence. Mixing them is how a healthy afternoon becomes a panic.

## Write the sentences, then the status icons

List the failures that can happen in your inbox and write the agent-facing line for each before you add icons.

- The reply did not send, and the draft remains.
- The address or the channel cannot receive it.
- The attachment or the macro blocked the send, and the text is kept.
- Someone else replied first, and the draft is kept.
- The thread did not load, and it is still in the queue.
- You are not sure the customer saw it, so the conversation stays unanswered.

Rehearse the lines with the sound of the queue on. A busy agent will not read a paragraph. Two sentences is the budget. If your line needs a third, the third is probably a cause you should have split into its own failure. Read them once in the voice you would use on a phone with the customer, and once in the voice you would use to a teammate. If those voices differ, the screen is mixing a customer apology with an internal diagnosis. Separate them. The agent can translate. The product should not make them translate under pressure.

Read each line as if you were on a shift. If you cannot tell whether the customer has the message, the line is not done. Color may support the line. An illustration may sit beside it only if the line remains the first thing on the screen. A mascot with a broken envelope, and the truth in a caption, is the pattern to avoid.

Then check the customer-facing side. A failure that is your fault should not become a customer-facing "we received your request" if you did not. Do not emit a cheerful automated receipt for a message you dropped. The agent's screen and the customer's inbox have to agree.

## Permissions wearing an error costume

Some failures are a role limit. The agent can read the thread and cannot refund, cannot see the card, or cannot reply on this channel. Those should say the limit and who can do the thing, not "request failed." [Permissions in a support inbox](/blog/permissions-in-a-support-inbox) is the next piece, because a hidden refund button feels like a bug, and a failed refund with no reason feels like one too.

Hanabi designs the failure states in the same Figma file as the sent state, with the draft still in the box. The build is Next.js, React, and TypeScript, with the message, its delivery state, and the draft stored so a refresh does not eat the reply. Prisma and PostgreSQL fit that record. Tailwind keeps the failed message visually quiet and still obvious. Motion can confirm a real send. It should not celebrate a guess.

If your agents retype replies because the screen threw them away, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The standard to borrow is simple: the interface keeps the work, and it says whether the other person saw it.
